In such a case, Bin Buffering has very large bins (8 times larger than Ola) which might be undesirable: the approximation power of Bin Buffering for range sums is at least 4 times lower than Ola because of the much larger bins. We have seen that Ola can have a competitive advantage when we are interested in getting approximate queries out of the memory buffer. Indeed, Ola supports a wide range of query types using a single memory buffer and relatively small bins. However, as with wavelet-based techniques {{cite:eec9aa0d3a7284dafe8f059a5fcc254c97061dbf}}, {{cite:0e2af1852f6c0f4c010a8d8fe165de4bc4088031}}, {{cite:02b263ec99a74822343d0ff348f8ccb053b6be31}}, Ola can support incrementally better estimates. With wavelet-based methods, one gets approximations by selecting the most significant wavelet coefficients. However, this approach calls for storing all coefficients in order to quickly answer queries within a user-specified error bound. This would be unacceptable for many applications: the wavelet buffer is as large as the external array itself. Incrementally better Ola approximations can be computed by first using the internal buffer, and then adding bins one by one. Indeed, for a given range query, the Ola algorithms involve many bins at both ends of the range. However, only the first few bins have a significant contribution. Recall subsection REF , in which we showed that {{formula:4e3469fc-ae98-4616-be7c-48545f11651f}} was given by {{formula:0d2f610f-f0c7-4b70-ae01-94a0c57431e8}} where {{formula:31fbd5f9-8e41-4642-bd9b-611a79919535}} is a Lagrange interpolation of the range query function {{formula:8a74838f-a0c1-416a-85d3-1178337efb8c}} . Only when the function {{formula:7e071825-878a-4305-8fb9-1313562be225}} goes from a polynomial to 0 is there a difference between the target range function {{formula:277e903e-7435-4e9b-a584-4663c5e28eb5}} and the range function {{formula:9b6d4df6-5202-4604-a583-bbe97d92aff6}} estimated by bin-wise Lagrange interpolation. However, the error made by Lagrange interpolation also diminishes as we move away from the bin containing the edge of the range. In many cases, it might be sufficient to take into account only 1 or 3 bins near the edge (at each endpoint of the range). For example, consider {{formula:b74f6063-a713-47fe-bf7f-27e63d19f785}} , {{formula:ae43c79d-d662-4b5c-b0e2-d28cf68bbc90}} with {{formula:3cc03909-f490-45c9-a37d-29c5b0262d27}} for {{formula:a4338820-e095-4a78-96c7-c98eda7b001b}} and 0 otherwise. A numerical evaluation shows that using only one bin at each endpoint instead of the required 3 will take care of 86% of the error when range edges are in the middle of a bin. The result is more significant for larger {{formula:651498a8-2b23-4167-bdd3-6124c24aa343}} , for example, for {{formula:e87c9754-eff6-41a4-bebe-439de91f1962}} , we need 15 bins at each endpoint for a complete evaluation; however, if we use only 5 centered, we take care of 97% of the error. (See Figure REF .) In short, Ola can provide wavelet-like progressive evaluation of the queries simply by querying fewer bins in the external array. We can analyze more mathematically the relationship between the number of bins used at each end of the range and the error. First note that bin-wise Lagrange interpolation is linear: if we interpolate the sequence {{formula:a595a895-45b1-4c14-801a-0db5ad47d95d}} and the sequence {{formula:77ce7320-2754-4c40-9de2-7e37ff91782f}} , then the sum of the two interpolants is just the interpolation of the sequence {{formula:6ed157bf-3dcd-412e-97cb-516f74a2bbca}} . Hence, it is sufficient to consider only one non-zero sample value at any given time. We proceed to show that the contribution of a sample value {{formula:7bab7378-a16c-49db-9ffa-ddd329ac460b}} to bin-wise Lagrange interpolation decays quickly past one bin. Let {{formula:2373713a-d9b1-4776-97a3-11285e704a41}} be fixed, and consider the interpolation of the sequence {{formula:c512770e-0f61-4486-b2e7-8e3029f88160}} , {{formula:bb06163d-a9a0-4a0e-98db-deab02ba0e20}} for all {{formula:52f499c9-31f6-4ef4-9e99-d6fc927a0544}} . We can then consider the interpolant {{formula:e5a8e810-833d-4a94-8a2b-8edb61eafa2d}} in the {{formula:71766955-dbe4-422c-b117-e778c595a0cf}} bin defined by the interval {{formula:0dbe5af3-95c1-4e91-a457-934489ecb359}} . Clearly the denominator will increase sharply in absolute value as {{formula:9b2989d5-574f-41a7-9f6e-2e29e8428a4b}} grows. We show that the numerator is non increasing in {{formula:4d16133f-43dd-4e70-932a-1a5d554a1373}} . Setting {{formula:f9199149-d4a3-4579-b663-87d4f9227445}} , we have {{formula:4fac8d27-568f-4156-9b73-4141a4793133}} . However, {{formula:9f57a09b-9eeb-4b6e-afff-c17278df147e}} and because {{formula:8345589d-734c-4a5a-b6ab-04b7e1223e3a}} , {{formula:c66a3895-c4a9-4e24-8995-7e5ac4975c1a}} and so, the numerator goes down in amplitude as {{formula:e988a5bf-ba12-4d4f-9f9e-bf8b0be642f5}} . On the other hand, the denominator in absolute value, {{formula:29ad62ce-e8d8-49bd-9776-2aa3272c37ab}} . Setting {{formula:3f63425d-076c-4f29-af28-7a06f72815d0}} , we have {{formula:f63f921d-e7d6-4fb4-9a56-0c5e229b99be}} which has a rate of increase of starting at {{formula:56add60e-a32f-4208-96be-c3debcd91320}} and rising with {{formula:21b2de06-083b-4c66-8223-0cd267d013d9}} . Hence, the amplitude of the polynomial decreases faster than exponentially as {{formula:a50cea20-2bc3-4245-be99-2d131b971936}} increases. It is difficult to compare the progressive approximation we get using this approach with related wavelet-based ones. Wavelet-based algorithms do not use the original array as a data source when answering queries and thus, they have much larger storage requirements. For large-scale applications, approximate queries are required for wavelet-based algorithms because storing all the coefficients is unthinkable whereas Ola has progressive approximate queries as an added option. {{figure:09d86f14-1aa1-417a-a5ee-5e25640eb88c}} This paper has considered bin-buffering algorithms and showed that using a hierarchical approach, highly scalable algebraic queries were possible even with a small buffer. Using overlapped bins, we have shown that we could buffer several local moments simultaneously and use much less storage than wavelet-based approaches while still supporting progressive queries and very scalable queries and updates. In short, we showed that {{formula:beb28896-8869-4852-86b6-6634bb8f6571}} local moments could be buffered using only a single real-valued buffer: using bins of a fixed size irrespective of {{formula:da296d68-b55a-4f67-89d0-27f235a52e9c}} . Other types of range queries could also be grouped and buffered efficiently together {{cite:3ef5da4a02bb793893168133bd5a62bb433cc576}}. By a direct product {{cite:aa49b595a8cf654ccc092582befe47263fd8efa8}}, Hierarchical Bin Buffering and therefore the Ola approach can be generalized to the multidimensional case. Some implementation issues were not addressed. For example, many forms of buffering using finite-accuracy floating-point numbers are susceptible to significant numerical errors. Finally, the source code used for the production of this paper is freely available {{cite:cdac3b577396445090fa52fc9f277b0d703ee418}}.

section_text: limitations: the communication graph is often assumed to be complete (or all-to-all), but in the absence of communication, the time-evolution of the systems' variables can be oscillatory or even chaotic. The system dynamics can be modified through the information exchange, and, as in the consensus problem, the goal of the interconnection is to reach synchronization to a common solution of the individual dynamics {{cite:8e3157379ef855482fcaf37fe9405ef51457a194}}, {{cite:684dc66e7d4a0631af50bd0baaeacb3bded11a07}}, {{cite:f2645858041eedb262e8cf7c96110637549c6792}}, {{cite:a21a35419d06741d5fa243f5c23f57f052b23620}}. Coordination problems encountered in the engineering world can often be rephrased as consensus or synchronization problems in which both the individual dynamics and the limited communication aspects play an important role. Designing interconnection control laws that can ensure synchronization of relevant variables is therefore a control problem that has attracted quite some attention in the recent years {{cite:3377176d8288814ff87c2dcfec20886d46780b65}}, {{cite:eb37f7114d6e7372c9c8d3c28bb100b08549eba5}}, {{cite:ae1621740a416c2873da35e86d33235d86024dc4}}, {{cite:032e7777248339fbdefded6f736f9ef54ceaf1f0}}, {{cite:fddc190ba04b15335e89d3e7f9f53df5b14d3eec}}. The present paper deals with a fairly general solution of the synchronization problem in the linear case. Assuming {{formula:736e8374-8f6f-4274-9cc6-d310fe71f3fa}} identical individual agents dynamics each described by the linear state-space model {{formula:2e1c1824-d387-447b-98b6-5f6625e21191}} , the main result is the construction of a dynamic output feedback controller that ensures exponential synchronization to a solution of the linear system {{formula:11890e3c-ed7f-4568-907c-9bbb4a824b68}} under the following assumptions: (i) {{formula:7a4cf05b-7fe9-4241-bd9f-c1b2f0d07340}} has no exponentially unstable mode, (ii) {{formula:69adb29b-ffa1-4408-889e-ae47c6506ba6}} is stabilizable and {{formula:7ada616a-9eb7-4725-9f61-896962265488}} is detectable, and (iii) the communication graph is uniformly connected. The result can be interpreted as a generalization of classical consensus algorithms, studied recently, corresponding to the particular case {{formula:b2c34407-09b6-4eb9-8873-58057cc5291b}} {{cite:0611b2b233fdc26e63788eca79cf783b27bc1c4b}}, {{cite:dffa2ea9c3c6665ef5522c572c54d2f0cecb647c}}. The generalization includes the non-trivial examples of synchronizing harmonic oscillators or chains of integrators. The proposed dynamic controller structure proposed in this paper differs from the static diffusive coupling often considered in the synchronization literature, which requires more stringent assumptions on the communication graph. For instance, the results in the recent paper {{cite:c1e1ffa3ebab1a8473177d4fd4cce2b7b0e7b4ff}} assume a time-invariant topology. The paper also provides sufficient conditions for synchronization by static diffusive coupling and illustrates on simple examples that synchronization may fail under diffusive coupling when the stronger assumptions on the communication graph are not satisfied. The paper is organized as follows. In Section the notation used throughout the paper is summarized, some preliminary results are reviewed and the synchronization problem is introduced and defined. In Section the linear case is studied when state coupling among the systems is allowed while in Section the output coupling case is considered. In Section we extend the main results to discrete-time linear systems and to periodic time-varying linear systems. Finally, in Section , two-dimensional examples are reported to illustrate the role of the proposed dynamic controller in situations where static diffusive coupling fails to achieve synchronization. section_text: Future work that studies this method with the inclusion of humans that help to validate and “clean" the recommended metadata would be telling of how much this method is able to speed up the process of generating accurate and reliable metadata for metadata-poor resources. Such an analysis is left to future research. Finally, multiplicative effects due to particle interaction may effect the results of the algorithm. For instance, if two particles, {{formula:259b42d2-baa5-450b-b757-10dec3ad9808}} and {{formula:6bc0533a-75fe-4e38-811f-39afda2f9096}} , meet at a particular node, {{formula:ce269697-9b00-45cc-853f-a1ecda243696}} , and {{formula:b85f1c22-1d44-44b3-ae8c-cc1e2f6946f8}} and {{formula:ad79b342-7582-4f30-9ed8-c6bf27d05b3a}} have similar metadata then the footprint they leave at {{formula:eabf6d95-a9d8-4b7e-a89b-774502603579}} should be more noticeable. Because two different metadata sources are supplying the same property values, there is an increased probability of that recommended metadata value being correct. Currently, only a summation is being provided. It may be interesting to multiply this summation by the number of unique particles that provided energy for a particular recommended metadata value. The variations of this preliminary framework will be explored in future work. Automatic metadata generation is becoming an increasingly important field of research as digital library repositories become more prevalent and move into the arena of less strongly controlled, decentralized collections (e.g. arXiv and CiteSeer). The creation and maintenance of high-quality, detailed metadata is hampered on numerous levels. Manual metadata creation methods are costly. Recent efforts to leverage the collective power of social tagging (i.e. “folksonomies") may address some of the shortcomings of the manual creation of metadata and result in viable models for online resources that do not require strongly controlled vocabularies and metadata ontologies. However, it is doubtful that “folksonomies" can be generalized to situations that require vetted, well-standardized metadata. The automated creation of metadata on the basis of content-analysis is a promising alternative to the manual creation of metadata. It is conceivably more efficient in situations where textual data is available and allows for more formal control of the type and nature of metadata that is extracted. However, it can be unreliable for non-text resources, yield low-quality metadata and can be computationally expensive. This article proposed another possible component of the metadata generation toolkit which may complement and support the above mentioned approaches. Instead of creating new metadata, metadata is propagated from a metadata-rich subset of the collection to similar, but metadata-poor subsets. The substrate for this extrapolation is an associative network of resource relations created from other available metadata. Metadata propagation may provide a computationally feasible means of generating large amounts of metadata for heterogeneous resources which can later be fine-tuned by manual intervention or cross-validation with content-based methods. The article finally provided experimental results using the High-Energy Physics bibliographic data set (hep-th 2003). Human intervention may play an important role in fine-tuning the metadata propagation algorithm. The results of this experiment are promising and there still exists a range of potential modifications to this basic framework that may lead to even better results. This research was financially supported by the Research Library at the Los Alamos National Laboratory. The modified hep-th 2003 bibliographic dataset was generously provided by Shou-de Lin and Jennifer H. Watkins provided editorial assistance. Finally, the hep-th 2003 database is based on data from the arXiv archive and the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center SPIRES-HEP database provided for the 2003 KDD Cup competition with additional preparation performed by the Knowledge Discovery Laboratory, University of Massachusetts Amherst.

section_text: open problems in S:openproblems, and conclude in S:conc. In this section we outline the physics that naturally leads us to consider Hankel hollow weighing matrices. For a more detailed discussion of the physics, see {{cite:4efe9dd016c2d263d418ae82099bd3cb8553ffa5}}, {{cite:56dc7cfcdebe51a8579d1e2db4a3600c1194d8fc}}, {{cite:3dd411ffa58524ec957504450bf4b0ff7688bc5d}}, {{cite:d056802759dcadf80d8c2aabd03c3bbbca179c4e}}. The resonant frequencies of an optical cavity are defined classically as the modes which constructively interfere inside the cavity. Because they are evenly spaced, they form a so-called a frequency comb. By placing a nonlinear medium inside the cavity, pump photons with frequency {{formula:06b8e4e9-9b60-4670-b38c-e6013b9642d0}} can downconvert into an entangled pair of photons, so long as the new photons' frequencies satisfy an energy conservation constraint, {{formula:61cb8668-cc6b-4cf4-af1c-cf318a8d881b}} where {{formula:8b83cce0-ff5e-48e7-9065-5462f97f3907}} and {{formula:4755ab92-e065-4513-a956-6907db8209d5}} are the {{formula:79e084d4-6c58-4a3d-b2a1-bf3b3d81c0ab}} and {{formula:db9c4c31-a13b-4e00-8f19-f4768563d908}} resonant frequencies of the cavity. The range over which the downconversion can occur is limited by the phasematching bandwidth of the cavity. More generally, multiple frequencies can be simultaneously phasematched inside the cavity, and upconversion is allowed as well as downconversion. The total Hamiltonian is then idealized by the following {{formula:5b7ef421-5039-436f-a14a-14c9017e8c47}} where {{formula:579ff936-9bd1-4d48-9076-5d75f051ab3a}} is the (discrete) spectrum of the polychromatic pump, {{formula:850f0442-2a18-4eb0-85a9-3d049fbf2f5c}} is a global coupling strength, {{formula:6e13caad-5aa3-47c8-9685-77681e87ddb9}} is the creation operator for the {{formula:a774e812-555e-401c-b889-ef3e2a7fa628}} mode, and {{formula:1e50ab33-0ad0-4070-a102-ead940c0bfd5}} are matrix elements of a symmetric matrix. In units of the fundamental frequency of the cavity, the restriction of the inner sum to terms with {{formula:a6bf9071-4f13-44fa-99e2-79c4339b860a}} enforces photon energy conservation, and the magnitude of {{formula:57922dd0-52d9-4d9e-896c-1a1b4f8f55ae}} determines the strength of the coupling in units of {{formula:d7ddafd8-7e1e-42d6-961d-7ba436849013}} , while the sign determines whether the photons are upconverted or downconverted. If all of the coupling strengths are equal, then {{formula:cc3e5396-b738-46c9-b2b0-cacd97d6e9cd}} is a Hankel matrix whose elements are either 0 or {{formula:467fe22b-4118-4b45-bd52-6adc950dc5a3}} , where {{formula:8dd1188d-07a4-4162-85e9-a12693c4f3e2}} is a constant. Experimental simplicity further demands that there is no single-mode squeezing and hence we require that the elements along the main diagonal of {{formula:43027b33-de55-40d9-9ce9-8f9bbb8f22d8}} are all zero, i.e. {{formula:0ff48cf1-93f4-4b22-9ba6-2c86a44040fb}} must be a hollow matrix. The Hamiltonian E:Hamiltonian can be used to create continuous-variable cluster states, defined as Gaussian states satisfying the relation {{formula:c13a3c0b-1ab6-4f74-bad5-d7cb72357953}} where {{formula:37d972ae-2e57-4866-aed6-7da7045feb17}} and {{formula:917705ef-a52f-4b7d-8b60-73ebc739d3e5}} are vectors of amplitude and phase quadratures for the {{formula:f69e45bd-899f-42d6-9514-dda2f7997639}} cavity mode, {{formula:b7e89264-299a-4bac-b7aa-890e2d13e9a0}} and {{formula:76a6c5ab-9706-4a3b-a52a-43a12cfaf220}} , {{formula:d0fc3f01-64d9-45a1-b76d-b4c7bb24c10e}} is the symmetric weighted adjacency matrix of the graph of the CVCS, and the arrow denotes the limit of large squeezing. Reference {{cite:56dc7cfcdebe51a8579d1e2db4a3600c1194d8fc}} first proved a nonunique relationship between the adjacency matrix {{formula:65254acd-a00f-40a7-9c56-ff1118aee2ee}} , which describes the cluster state, and the adjacency matrix {{formula:2be4014c-0566-4c10-b14e-5dacd5b33cfb}} , which describes the coupling between the modes inside the cavity. The general relationship is somewhat complicated, so references {{cite:3dd411ffa58524ec957504450bf4b0ff7688bc5d}}, {{cite:4efe9dd016c2d263d418ae82099bd3cb8553ffa5}}, {{cite:d056802759dcadf80d8c2aabd03c3bbbca179c4e}} introduced the simplifying ansatz that {{formula:97d162fe-0b8e-41b4-97b6-f1a9bb98d66a}} from which it follows {{cite:3dd411ffa58524ec957504450bf4b0ff7688bc5d}}, {{cite:d056802759dcadf80d8c2aabd03c3bbbca179c4e}} that (up to a trivial relabeling) {{formula:c22842cb-b6de-44f0-9fe3-4f90128bee15}} In short, assuming {{formula:d9219d87-704c-4b1a-87a4-66c929b39fa9}} is an orthogonal matrix implies the graph describing the couplings between photons in the cavity ({{formula:afc3fa8e-4297-4a36-8182-0345fd262ce3}} ) is identical to the graph describing the cluster state ({{formula:2b30f2fc-18b9-45f3-8dd8-a55947fd8bd3}} ), which is a vast simplification over the general relationship. The derivation requires that {{formula:7df42901-2524-4fd2-a9b5-33b8129a0870}} be the adjacency matrix of a bipartite graph, but as we will see, one can derive this from the Hankel and hollow constraints. We now see how the twin demands of experimental and theoretical simplicity for creating CVCS in an optical cavity naturally lead us to consider Hankel hollow orthogonal matrices, all of whose non-zero elements are either {{formula:f56bc9c3-8b2f-4d8d-9fa9-86fb372f95d5}} , for some constant {{formula:cfbe24b8-6a48-48f6-b142-bcae64e00c9f}} . We can of course consider renormalized matrices instead by dividing out {{formula:6f510777-bb3c-4198-831b-c20d958b1363}} , so that all entries are {{formula:2045d900-7805-496c-8ac0-131dc2a6e1c8}} ; after finding these renormalized matrices, we can then reintroduce the constant afterwards so that E:Asquared holds. Thus, we see that finding and classifying Hankel hollow weighing matrices is our primary interest. For completeness, we mention one further elaboration that is possible for this scheme. If the photons' polarization, transverse, or spatial degrees of freedom are taken into account, then the Hamiltonian E:Hamiltonian can be modified by adding additional indices for these modes. If these additional modes are all frequency-degenerate, then an additional sum over these degenerate modes appears in E:Hamiltonian, which allows for the symmetric intercoupling between the degenerate degrees of freedom. If such an interaction could be simultaneously phasematched by the nonlinear medium inside the cavity, then one is naturally lead to consider block-Hankel matrices, where the size of the blocks is equal to the number of degenerate degrees of freedom. We leave the consideration of block-Hankel hollow weighing matrices to future work. In this section we introduce the definition of anticirculant graphs and study some of their first properties. For the sake of self-containedness, we will define here all the graph-theoretic concepts we require. For further background on theory of graphs the interested reader is referred to the book by Diestel {{cite:24838f6f33b693e443cca46373d1dde0692fc3bd}}. Our reference about permutations and finite groups is Cameron {{cite:c4e07fc53a27594c2be294b50923af92574cccf3}}. We will work with simple graphs. A (simple) graph {{formula:4c649e43-0efc-4b81-8e59-7e7f559ea683}} is an ordered pair of sets defined as follows: {{formula:9de57558-cb27-4303-b380-b4e43544c8f8}} is a non-empty set, whose elements are called vertices; {{formula:b30f0d9c-e794-419a-b604-13950e9d87e5}} is a non-empty set of unordered pairs of vertices, whose elements are called edges. An edge of the form {{formula:25dd71ed-6449-47d0-b532-c29ffb934aa3}} is called a loop. Two vertices {{formula:10b5f563-17a8-4b31-ab5a-8adbb3c1d38f}} and {{formula:f971293d-3e5b-4ab1-b716-c42354fbca42}} are said to be adjacent if {{formula:d4f1597e-6e44-45cf-9b04-40ca9747e2d1}} . Often, this is simply denoted by writing {{formula:9625e869-1d8d-4b73-91d7-b2579b755ce5}} . A graph is loopless if it is has no loops. The adjacency matrix of a graph {{formula:d566257e-35f5-4ddc-b733-386808d58b05}} is denoted by {{formula:39665e85-baa4-4a47-8ebe-fbcda9bbb7bf}} and defined by {{formula:02303df8-2fba-4303-a5a7-cad246cd509a}} An adjacency matrix of a loopless graph is said to be hollow. Table 1 provides a summary of the methods discussed in detail below. {{table:67942bf9-1a5d-4406-b397-f7379833015d}} The most straightforward way to age-date an individual brown dwarf is to borrow from its environment, a tactic that is suitable for members of coeval clusters/associations and companions to age-dated stars. Brown dwarfs are well-sampled down to and below the deuterium fusing mass limit (M {{formula:c8a349ce-636d-43f4-bab2-0cb3319d7cb6}} 0.013 M{{formula:d0fbbffc-95bf-4633-b5e8-9575ac78911e}} ) in the youngest nearby clusters ({{formula:948f7e90-0ecc-489d-8b26-ecbb263678db}} {{formula:8c2f00e5-7217-4422-877c-a1eb14475eda}} 5 Myr), as their luminosities are greater at early ages. Brown dwarfs have also been identified in somewhat older (10–50 Myr)“loose associations” in the vicinity of the Sun ({{formula:9cfa10b6-30cb-4031-897f-5c96275e3bde}} {{formula:9cbdbdfb-ef9b-4aea-befe-84be9eb2f8c5}} 50–100 pc; e.g., {{cite:15f44987c00c2b2c90a1607b6160c901c1aec91a}}). For older and more distant clusters ({{formula:83b41c4b-48c1-487a-a353-8178d9b31b89}} {{formula:690b614b-3bd5-4319-b3ff-87fa70b66e4b}} 1 kpc), decreasing surface temperatures and compact radii exacerbate the sensitivity issues that plague low-mass stellar studies (see contribution by G. Piotto). There are as yet no known brown dwarfs in globular clusters, despite detection of the end of the stellar main sequence in systems such as NGC 6397 {{cite:c3aec005bae16b8b016b152ed6e95e913ebbba61}}. For brown dwarfs in young clusters, numerous studies have examined age-related trends in colors (e.g., {{cite:ed91b8da3b41f6438d06892edbbf3ee46a47aada}}), spectral characteristics (e.g., {{cite:6d02497190066bfb3e6db4becc621e12240d8bfe}}), accretion timescales (e.g., {{cite:5824d928b0c3153c36288041e9f25861d4c851ec}}) and circum(sub)stellar disk evolution (e.g., {{cite:06ee4a9220fefb3f0be20346894f41b1319014a5}}). These have been coarsely quantified, and appear to be most useful at very young ages ({{formula:f6f71487-1f38-401e-93b1-b41140900d04}} 10 Myr). Surface properties and luminosities are highly variable at these ages due to sensitivity to formation conditions (e.g., {{cite:c5cc0a11710490811486e6b9d14804e54b1b53bd}}), ongoing accretion, complex magnetic effects (e.g., {{cite:fc93e941df80ffc048a92610918a627d5cad904c}}) and age spreads within a cluster (see contribution by R. Jeffries). Hence, while brown dwarfs in clusters with ages spanning {{formula:d04cab8f-1ad5-4f29-8829-12127be65e27}} 1–650 Myr are now well-documented, with age uncertainties as good as 10% (for the LDB technique; see {{formula:2752efcf-bf12-4728-b9ad-906588d5f8b6}} 3), useful predictive trends are probably limited to ages of {{formula:0e4883ac-4a31-445b-9a11-524283ca5db6}} 10 Myr. Known brown dwarf companions to main sequence stars now number a few dozen, spanning a wide range of separation, age and composition. Many of these systems are widely-separated so that their brown dwarf companions can be directly studied. Age uncertainties for companion brown dwarfs depend on stellar dating methods which are generally more uncertain (50–100%; e.g., {{cite:2846bd411a46d3033c7ace28d4b8d255ace1785e}}) than cluster ages. Searches for substellar companions to more precisely age-dated white dwarfs (e.g. {{cite:83e6d0a5494a6f0fdbad6697a9c46cf831bf1a6a}}, {{cite:c27d7df5faca8aba6723804766afa5a4e49bba75}}) and subgiants {{cite:b8139efc3091db6b2604210afb1c5ed65573ba4f}} have so far met with limited success. Nevertheless, brown dwarf companions to age-dated stars serve as important benchmarks for calibrating other age-dating methods at late ages ({{formula:c75a3202-9e01-42fa-92f1-9c09a435267b}} 500 Myr) and are fundamental for testing evolutionary models (see contribution by T. Dupuy). Lithium is fused at a lower temperature than hydrogen (2.5{{formula:cf67f965-09e2-493d-b267-4b03c1ec73e8}} 10{{formula:891d6978-1c0c-4d95-921f-01f3ef3a86f9}} K), resulting in a somewhat lower fusing mass limit (0.065 M{{formula:dbed2bf3-07ce-4e0b-a1e9-b6f2b17b6542}} ; {{cite:e56827c6774e756dc66db9a31d4182ddfe03b275}}). Because the interiors of low mass stars and brown dwarfs are fully convective at early ages, an object with a mass above this limit will fully deplete its initial reservoir of lithium within {{formula:1e5696d9-60b2-4638-a668-65e4af396991}} 200 Myr. Hence, any system older than this which exhibits Li I absorption has a mass less than 0.065 M{{formula:0be468ff-5122-4aa7-93dc-3031536f4187}} and is therefore a brown dwarf (e.g., {{cite:0c902710e5720aec64c89f9b33a6ff410227a8fb}}). With a mass limit, one can use evolutionary models to determine an age limit. In the age range {{formula:b02712a0-f638-44bc-a613-fab77a625628}} 10–200 Myr, the degree of lithium depletion in low-mass stars and brown dwarfs is itself mass-dependent, occurring earlier in more massive stars which first achieve the necessary core temperatures. Hence, over this range the age of an individual source can be precisely constrained if its mass is known. A more practical approach, however, is to ascertain the age of a group of coeval low-mass objects based on which sources do or do not exhibit Li I absorption; this is the lithium depletion boundary (LDB) technique. Different evolutionary models yield remarkably similar predictions for the location of the LDB over a broad range of ages {{cite:941cd1870230b9e4d007f12acad1b516f7fd9d17}}, and the boundary itself is readily identifiable in color-magnitude diagrams. As such, this technique has been used to age-date several nearby young clusters and associations (e.g., {{cite:5f4c473f4a626eb7b813da038e19762f25362cdb}}, {{cite:0aa86035ed3570d1faf6a667580310e96f3752cd}}, {{cite:a539d773f3285dc40c56bb63d2d2755c693ea5b3}}, {{cite:d0ed153c67c33b36fcac16e67b9643f6e70c7998}}). LDB studies have also provided independent confirmation of other cluster-dating methods such as isochrone fitting {{cite:a539d773f3285dc40c56bb63d2d2755c693ea5b3}}. A variant of the LDB technique for coeval binary systems has been proposed by {{cite:17984f83a2310cd48d75b477084a8897b2300087}}, in which a system that exhibits Li I absorption in the secondary but not in the primary can have both lower and upper age limits assigned to it (note that the presence/absence of Li I in both components simply sets a single upper/lower age limit). This technique requires resolved optical spectroscopy of both components and can be pursued only for a few (rare) wide low-mass pairs (e.g., Burgasser et al., in prep.) or using high spatial-resolution spectroscopy (e.g. {{cite:09db6dfd8019c882d6da74c45a9487139c06e08b}}). No single brown dwarf pair straddling the LDB has yet been identified. Despite its utility, the detection of LI I absorption in brown dwarf spectra has limitations. The 6708 Å line lies in an relatively faint spectral region for cool L-type dwarfs, so sensitive spectral observations on large telescopes are typically required to detect (or convincingly rule out) this feature. For optically-brighter M-type brown dwarfs, high-resolution observations are generally required to distinguish Li I absorption from overlapping molecular absorption features. Young brown dwarfs ({{formula:87369e06-cec4-46cc-8511-286c1e16ef36}} 50 Myr) with low surface gravities show weakened alkali line absorption (see {{formula:df33d6ef-3020-4acf-809e-f839464296be}} 5), including Li I, making it again necessary to obtain sensitive, high-resolution observations {{cite:15f44987c00c2b2c90a1607b6160c901c1aec91a}}. For brown dwarfs cooler than {{formula:e0c2aa9c-6148-4794-8b6d-b3243dc501a3}} 1500 K (i.e., the T dwarfs), lithium is chemically depleted in the photosphere through its conversion to LiCl, LiF or LiOH {{cite:58bb262fbbae7790bd0028d0996a7cd72afdc9fb}}.
